name: Finding Acquisition Targets
title: Finding Acquisition Targets
answer: Finding acquisition targets is the front end of private equity and corporate development work: deciding which companies a buyer should approach, and why, before any valuation or negotiation begins. It covers the whole funnel from setting a thesis, through screening a market, to building a shortlist and making first contact. The output is not a deal but a ranked set of candidates with a reason to pursue each one, plus the evidence behind that ranking. It sits between strategy, which says what kind of company to buy, and diligence, which tests whether a specific company is worth the price.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Finding acquisition targets is the front end of private equity and corporate development work: deciding which companies a buyer should approach, and why, before any valuation or negotiation begins. It covers the whole funnel from setting a thesis, through screening a market, to building a shortlist and making first contact. The output is not a deal but a ranked set of candidates with a reason to pursue each one, plus the evidence behind that ranking. It sits between strategy, which says what kind of company to buy, and diligence, which tests whether a specific company is worth the price.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is company data: registries and filings, ownership records, patent and trademark databases, job postings, web and app activity, news, and paid databases such as PitchBook, Capital IQ, Crunchbase and Dealroom. Teams keep a CRM of past approaches and a pipeline of live conversations, often in tools like Salesforce or Affinity, and increasingly a data warehouse that joins these sources into one view of a company. AI enters as search and matching over that pile, using embeddings to find companies similar to a known good target and language models to read filings, websites and press at a scale no analyst team could. The constraint is rarely compute. It is data access, licensing terms and the fact that private company information is patchy and stale.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with a thesis expressed as criteria: sector, size, geography, growth, ownership, and strategic fit. Analysts then build a long list from databases and screens, deduplicate it, and score candidates against the criteria. AI changes the middle of this process by ranking and clustering candidates, extracting structured facts from unstructured text, and flagging companies that resemble past successful deals or that show signals such as hiring surges or new facilities. A human still validates every shortlist, because a model cannot see a founder's reluctance to sell or a customer relationship about to lapse. Outreach and relationship building remain manual, and the judgment about whether a target is genuinely available is made by people, not scores.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Sourcing runs on confidential and sometimes personal data, so teams work under database licences, non disclosure agreements and, in Europe, rules on personal data that limit how contact and ownership information can be stored and reused. Using AI to screen candidates raises questions of provenance: where did this fact come from, when was it last true, and can it be shown to an investment committee. Bias matters too, since a model trained on past deals will keep proposing the same kinds of companies and quietly narrow the funnel. Firms handle this with source citations, audit trails, human sign off on shortlists, and clear rules on what may be fed to external models. Nothing here is legal advice, and specific obligations depend on jurisdiction and fund structure.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward continuous, always on sourcing rather than periodic list building: systems that watch a defined market, surface new companies as they appear, and update scores as signals change. Expect tighter integration between sourcing tools and diligence workflows, so that evidence gathered at the top of the funnel carries through to the deal file. Agent style tools that draft outreach and assemble company profiles are already appearing, with humans kept on the decision. The open questions are data rights, model transparency and whether faster screening actually improves returns or just produces longer lists. The firms that benefit most will be those that treat sourcing data as an asset with clear ownership and quality standards.
